prose: `{variable}` has {k} levels ({levels}). R uses {reference_level} as the baseline and adds {n_dummy} indicator column(s); each coefficient is the difference from {reference_level}, not that group's own mean.
`{variable}` has {k} levels ({levels}). With no intercept it is entered as cell means: each coefficient is that level's expected response directly.

`{variable}` has {k} levels ({levels}) under sum-to-zero contrasts. Coefficients are deviations from the grand mean and there is no single reference level; use group_means() for the group-by-group picture.
`{variable}` has {k} levels ({levels}) under Helmert contrasts. Each coefficient compares a level to the mean of the earlier levels; there is no single reference level.
`{variable}` has {k} ordered levels ({levels}) under polynomial contrasts. Coefficients are linear, quadratic and higher-order trends, not level-to-level differences.
`{variable}` has {k} levels ({levels}) under a custom contrast matrix. Read each coefficient against its contrast column, and use group_means() for the group means.
The slope of {cont} changes across levels of {fac}. The coefficient table reports differences in slope from the reference group; the per-group slopes below give each group's actual slope.
The effect of {fac_a} depends on {fac_b} (a difference of differences). The cells below give each combination's expected response directly, so you do not have to add coefficients by hand.
The slope of {cont_a} changes with {cont_b}. Use group_slopes(at = ...) to read the slope at chosen values of {cont_b}.
This model has no factor predictors, so there is no dummy (contrast) coding to explain. Continuous predictors are read directly from their coefficients.
